phil:wittgenstein: Ludwig Wittgenstein was an Austrian-British philosopher whose work reshaped the philosophy of language, logic, and mind across the twentieth century. In his early Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus he argued that meaningful language pictures the structure of the world and that many traditional philosophical problems dissolve once the limits of sense are drawn. His later Philosophical Investigations repudiated much of this, holding that meaning arises from use within shared "language-games" and "forms of life," and attacking the idea of a private language. Both phases treated philosophy less as doctrine than as a therapeutic clarification of the confusions bred by our own words.
phil:russell: Bertrand Russell was a British philosopher, logician, and public intellectual who helped found analytic philosophy. With Alfred North Whitehead he wrote Principia Mathematica, an ambitious attempt to derive mathematics from logic, and his theory of descriptions showed how apparently referring phrases like "the present King of France" could be analyzed without positing dubious entities. He wrote widely on knowledge, mind, and metaphysics, defending logical atomism and empiricism, and later became famous for essays on ethics, religion, education, and pacifism, winning the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1950.
phil:moore: G.E. Moore was a British philosopher and a central figure in early analytic philosophy alongside Russell. In ethics he argued that "good" is a simple, indefinable property and coined the "naturalistic fallacy" against attempts to define it in natural terms, while his "open question argument" tested any proposed definition of the good. In epistemology he defended common sense against skepticism, most famously by insisting he could know he had hands, and his careful, deflationary method of analysis strongly influenced the style of twentieth-century philosophy.
phil:frege: Gottlob Frege was a German mathematician and logician widely regarded as the founder of modern logic and a father of analytic philosophy. He invented a formal system of quantified logic that superseded Aristotelian syllogistic and pursued logicism, the project of grounding arithmetic in logic. His distinction between the sense (Sinn) and reference (Bedeutung) of expressions became foundational to the philosophy of language, and though his logical system was shown vulnerable to Russell's paradox, his conceptual innovations transformed logic, mathematics, and semantics.
phil:quine: W.V.O. Quine was an American philosopher and logician who was among the most influential figures in twentieth-century analytic philosophy. In "Two Dogmas of Empiricism" he attacked the analytic-synthetic distinction and reductionism, arguing instead for a holistic picture in which our beliefs face experience as a connected web. He defended a naturalized epistemology continuous with science, advanced the thesis of the indeterminacy of translation, and pressed influential views on ontological commitment captured by his slogan "to be is to be the value of a bound variable."
phil:kripke: Saul Kripke was an American philosopher and logician who made landmark contributions to modal logic, the philosophy of language, and metaphysics. As a teenager he helped develop the possible-worlds semantics for modal logic, and in Naming and Necessity he argued that names are "rigid designators" referring to the same object across possible worlds, introducing the idea of necessary a posteriori and contingent a priori truths. He also offered an influential, skeptical reading of Wittgenstein on rule-following, reshaping debates about meaning and normativity.
phil:lewis: David Lewis was an American philosopher known for systematic work of great scope across metaphysics, language, mind, and logic. He is most famous for modal realism, the striking view that all logically possible worlds exist as concrete as our own, which he used to analyze possibility, causation, and counterfactuals. He also developed influential accounts of conventions, laws of nature as the theorems of the best deductive system, and mental states as functional roles, combining bold theses with rigorous argument.
phil:ryle: Gilbert Ryle was a British philosopher associated with ordinary-language philosophy at Oxford. In The Concept of Mind he attacked what he called the "dogma of the ghost in the machine"—the Cartesian picture of mind as an inner, non-physical substance—diagnosing it as a "category mistake" that misconstrues mental talk. He argued that many mental concepts refer to dispositions and patterns of behavior rather than hidden inner episodes, a view that helped shape behaviorist and functionalist approaches to the mind.
phil:jackson: Frank Jackson is an Australian philosopher best known for the "knowledge argument" against physicalism about the mind. His thought experiment about Mary, a scientist who knows every physical fact about color vision but has only seen black and white, asks whether she learns something new upon first seeing red—suggesting there are non-physical facts of experience. Jackson later revised his own conclusions, and he has also done influential work on conditionals, ethics, and the methodology of conceptual analysis.
phil:nagel: Thomas Nagel is an American philosopher who has written on mind, ethics, and political philosophy with a persistent concern for the tension between subjective and objective standpoints. His essay "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" argued that the subjective, first-person character of conscious experience resists reduction to physical description, sharpening the mind-body problem. In The View from Nowhere and elsewhere he explored how to reconcile our particular, engaged perspective with the impersonal view that reason and science seem to demand.
phil:parfit: Derek Parfit was a British philosopher regarded as one of the most important moral philosophers of his era. In Reasons and Persons he argued that personal identity over time consists in psychological continuity rather than a deep further fact, with far-reaching consequences for self-interest, rationality, and our obligations to future generations. In On What Matters he sought to reconcile major ethical traditions—Kantian, contractualist, and consequentialist—and defended a robust moral realism about objective, mind-independent reasons.
phil:mctaggart: J.M.E. McTaggart was a British idealist philosopher best remembered for his argument for the unreality of time. He distinguished the "A-series," which orders events as past, present, and future, from the "B-series," which orders them as earlier and later, and contended that the A-series is both essential to time and internally contradictory, concluding that time itself is illusory. His argument continues to frame contemporary debates in the metaphysics of time.
phil:clark: Andy Clark is a British philosopher of mind and cognitive science known for advancing embodied, embedded, and extended approaches to cognition. With David Chalmers he proposed the "extended mind" thesis, arguing that tools and external resources can literally form part of a person's cognitive processes rather than merely aiding them. He has also been a leading interpreter of predictive-processing theories, on which the brain is fundamentally a prediction machine minimizing error against incoming sensory evidence.
phil:vann-inwagen: Peter van Inwagen is an American philosopher who has made influential contributions to metaphysics, free will, and philosophy of religion. In An Essay on Free Will he articulated the "consequence argument," a widely discussed case for incompatibilism holding that free will is inconsistent with determinism. He is also known for a distinctive view in the metaphysics of material objects, according to which the only composite things that exist are living organisms, and for careful work on the problem of evil.
phil:bergson: Henri Bergson was a French philosopher whose work on time, consciousness, and life brought him wide fame in the early twentieth century and the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1927. He distinguished measurable, spatialized clock-time from "duration" (durée), the qualitative, flowing character of lived experience, and argued that intuition can grasp what analytic intellect fragments. His notion of the "élan vital," a creative impulse driving evolution and change, made him a central figure in process and vitalist thought.
